claims.text: Sequential cryo-rolling followed by controlled partial-recrystallization annealing can produce a heterogeneous microstructure in the named multi-principal-element alloy families.
The proposed microstructure contains coarse grains, ultrafine grains, and coherent nanoprecipitates.
The hierarchical microstructure simultaneously maximizes yield strength and tensile ductility through back-stress hardening and strain-gradient effects.
The initial alloy may be an as-cast or homogenized Co-Cr-Ni-based alloy or AlCoCrFeNi2.1 with a coarse-grained single-phase or eutectic-lamellar structure.
The initial alloy exhibits room-temperature brittleness or low ductility.
Multi-pass rolling at 77 K to 80–90% thickness reduction, followed by annealing at 800–900 °C for about 1 hour and water quenching, is an applicable processing schedule.
Cryogenic rolling suppresses dynamic recovery and preserves a high dislocation density.
Intermediate short annealing selectively recrystallizes only part of the deformed matrix and preserves a heterogeneous grain structure.
Low-temperature aging can introduce L12 nanoprecipitates when permitted by alloy composition.
The resulting coarse grains are 10–30 μm and the ultrafine grains are 0.5–2 μm.
Coarse unrecrystallized grains act as soft domains, while ultrafine recrystallized grains or nanotwins act as hard domains.
Load partitioning between hard and soft domains generates geometrically necessary dislocations at their interfaces.
The interfacial dislocations generate long-range internal back-stresses that sustain strain hardening.
Soft domains accommodate plastic deformation and delay necking, while hard domains and precipitates provide yield strength.
Low stacking-fault energy promotes deformation twins or stacking faults that dynamically refine the structure and prevent premature failure.
The treated alloy will have yield strength above 1.4 GPa and uniform tensile ductility above 12–14%.
The treated alloy will outperform both the as-cast state and homogeneous ultrafine-grained counterparts in the combined strength–ductility response.
The stress–strain response will exhibit a distinct Region II upturn in strain-hardening rate rather than a monotonic decrease.
Homogeneous ultrafine-grained counterparts can retain high strength but have very low uniform ductility.
The strategy is primarily effective in low-stacking-fault-energy alloys and may fail in high-stacking-fault-energy alloys because full dislocations recover readily.

contradictions.description: An anneal at 900 °C for 1 hour is included in the proposed partial-recrystallization window, but approximately the same treatment is also presented as a full-recrystallization control. Whether it is partial or full must be specified for the particular alloy.

The initial state is characterized as brittle or low-ductility, although one cited AlCoCrFeNi2.1 as-cast state has about 17% elongation, which is higher than the approximately 14% elongation reported after cryo-rolling and annealing.
